standard.title: Explain historical interpretations
standard.description: explain historical interpretations about significant events, individuals and groups
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify perspectives, attitudes, and values of the past in sources (AC9HH7S06). They have not yet applied the concept of historical interpretation — understanding that historians construct different interpretations of the same events, that interpretations are argument-based rather than simply 'what happened', and that explaining why different interpretations exist is a distinct historical skill.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain historical interpretations about significant events, individuals, and groups — demonstrating understanding that interpretations are constructed from evidence and argument, that different interpretations of the same event can coexist, and that developing a historical argument about why something is interpreted in different ways is a key historical skill.

nodes.label: What is a historical interpretation?
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what a historical interpretation is — that it is a constructed argument about the past based on evidence, not a simple statement of fact — and distinguish between a historical fact and a historical interpretation.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain the difference between a historical fact (verifiable from evidence) and a historical interpretation (an argument about meaning, significance, or causation constructed from evidence), and give an example of each.
nodes.typical_width: Explain that historical interpretations are constructed arguments about significant events, individuals, or groups — that historians use evidence to build cases for particular understandings of the past, and that the same evidence can support different interpretations. Distinguish clearly between facts (what the evidence directly shows) and interpretations (what the evidence is taken to mean).
wider: Examine a specific example where historical interpretation has changed over time — such as the interpretation of the fall of Rome, the significance of Alexander the Great, or the legacy of a First Nations leader — and analyse why the interpretation changed (new evidence, changed values, new questions).
Investigate the concept of historiography — the history of historical writing — and examine how different historians in different periods have interpreted the same event differently.
Explore what makes a historical interpretation strong or weak — examining criteria such as use of evidence, logical reasoning, accounting for counter-evidence, and consistency with established facts.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate facts with interpretations will treat competing historical interpretations as factual disagreements rather than constructed arguments in N2 — the analysis of why interpretations differ requires understanding that they are arguments, not rival facts.

response_modes.reason: The distinction between historical fact and historical interpretation is conceptually demanding for Year 7 students, who frequently conflate them. The reasoning scaffold — this is what the evidence directly shows (fact) vs this is the argument the historian constructs about what it means (interpretation) — needs to be made explicit with concrete examples before students can apply it reliably.

success_criteria: Correctly defines historical interpretation as a constructed argument about the past, not a statement of fact.
Distinguishes between a historical fact and a historical interpretation, with an example of each.
Explains that interpretations are based on evidence — they are reasoned arguments, not opinions.

nodes.label: Different interpretations of the same event or individual
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how the same historical event, individual, or group can be interpreted in different ways by different historians, and explain what causes these differences — including different evidence, different questions, and different values.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe two different interpretations of the same event or individual and identify at least one reason why the interpretations differ.
nodes.typical_width: Describe two or more different interpretations of the same historical event, individual, or group — explaining how different historians have constructed different arguments about significance, causation, or legacy — and explain what causes the differences: different evidence available, different questions being asked, different values and perspectives of the historians themselves.
wider: Examine different interpretations of the short-term triggers and turning points of a historical decline — such as the decline of an empire or ancient society — identifying the evidence and reasoning behind each interpretation.

Investigate how the same individual (e.g. Alexander the Great, Caesar, a First Nations historical figure) has been interpreted very differently in different historical periods and by historians from different national or cultural traditions.
Explore how contested interpretations are resolved — or not — in historical scholarship, examining how historians respond to competing interpretations through evidence, argument, and debate.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly accept a single interpretation as 'the answer' and find it difficult to hold multiple interpretations simultaneously. Exposure to multiple, genuinely different interpretations of the same event or individual — each with different evidence and reasoning — builds the understanding that interpretive diversity is inherent to historical knowledge rather than a sign of historical confusion. Breadth across different historical figures and events is what develops this as a general understanding rather than a one-off example.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The examination of competing historical interpretations is intellectually rich — it connects source analysis, perspective, causation, and the nature of historical knowledge into a single analytical task. Advancing students can engage with historiography, the sociology of historical knowledge production, and the methodological debates that drive historical scholarship forward. This is also one of the most directly relevant skills for senior history study.
success_criteria: Describes at least two different interpretations of the same event or individual.
Identifies at least two reasons why the interpretations differ (not just 'they had different opinions').
Does not treat one interpretation as simply 'right' — recognises that multiple interpretations can coexist legitimately.

nodes.label: Developing a historical argument about interpretation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop a historical argument about why an event, individual, or group is interpreted in different ways — constructing a reasoned explanation that accounts for the different interpretations and the factors that produce them.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop a basic argument explaining why a specific historical event or individual is interpreted in different ways, identifying at least two factors that produce the different interpretations.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a historical argument explaining why a specific historical event, individual, or group is interpreted in different ways — identifying the different interpretations, explaining the evidence and reasoning behind each, and constructing a reasoned account of why interpretive diversity exists for this case. Connect the argument to the factors identified in Node 2 (evidence, questions, values).
wider: Develop an argument about which of two competing interpretations is better supported by evidence — constructing a case for one interpretation while acknowledging the strengths of the alternative.

Investigate how historical arguments about interpretation function as a genre — examining the structure, evidence use, and reasoning in a published historical argument, and applying those structural insights to student argument development.

Explore how developing arguments about historical interpretation connects to the S08 communicating skill — examining how the argument structure developed in this descriptor supports the creation of historical writing.

response_modes.reason: This node integrates understanding of what interpretations are (Node 1) and why they differ (Node 2) into the descriptor's full demand — developing a historical argument about interpretation. Students must coordinate interpretation identification, causal analysis of interpretive diversity, and argument construction into a coherent explanatory claim. This is the most demanding node in the S-strand to this point, and directly prepares S08.

success_criteria: Develops a reasoned argument — not just a description — about why a historical event or individual is interpreted in different ways.
Identifies at least two interpretations and at least two factors producing the difference.
The argument uses evidence to support its claims, not just assertion.
